title: API Comparison: Setup and Custom Lattice Structure
content: The file opens with a detailed docstring stating the open question (is `Lattice n` equivalent to `Module.Basis (Fin n) ℝ (Fin n → ℝ)`?) and its answer (YES). The imports bring in `ZLattice.Basic` (Mathlib's ZSpan machinery), `PiL2` (inner product space infrastructure for `Fin n → ℝ`), `Matrix.Basis` (change-of-basis lemmas), and `Matrix.Determinant.Basic`. The namespace `MinkowskiFundamentalTheoremOQ04` keeps this file self-contained. The `structure Lattice` at lines 41–44 defines the custom type used throughout: a matrix `basis : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ` together with a proof `basis_invertible : basis.det ≠ 0`, encoding invertibility as a proof term rather than an `Invertible` typeclass instance.
mathContext: Custom type: $\text{Lattice}\, n = \{\, (B,\, h) \mid B \in \mathbf{M}_{n\times n}(\mathbb{R}),\; h : \det(B) \neq 0 \,\}$. Mathlib type: $\text{Module.Basis}(\text{Fin}\,n, \mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R}^n)$, which is a linear equivalence $\mathbb{R}^{\text{Fin}\,n} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb{R}^n$ (definitionally). The question is whether these types are in canonical bijection.

title: Key Lemma: Every Basis Matrix Has Nonzero Determinant
content: Part 1 contains two theorems. First, `piBasicFun_toMatrix_eq_transpose` (lines 54–60) establishes that for the standard basis `e = Pi.basisFun ℝ (Fin n)`, the change-of-basis matrix satisfies `e.toMatrix b = (Matrix.of b)ᵀ`. The proof is a single `simp` call: `e.repr (b j) i = (b j) i` by `Pi.basisFun_repr`, which is exactly `(Matrix.of b)ᵀ i j`. Second, `basis_matrix_det_ne_zero` (lines 62–76) is the key lemma enabling the whole equivalence. It proves `(Matrix.of b).det ≠ 0` for any `Module.Basis (Fin n) ℝ (Fin n → ℝ)`. The proof uses `Basis.toMatrix_mul_toMatrix_flip b e = 1`, takes determinants (`Matrix.det_mul`, `Matrix.det_one`), substitutes `e.toMatrix b = (Matrix.of b)ᵀ` and applies `Matrix.det_transpose` to get `det(b.toMatrix e) · det(Matrix.of b) = 1`. If `det(Matrix.of b) = 0` then `0 = 1`, contradiction.
mathContext: Let $e = \mathrm{Pi.basisFun}\,\mathbb{R}\,(\mathrm{Fin}\,n)$ be the standard basis for $\mathbb{R}^n = \mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \mathbb{R}$. Step 1: $e.\mathrm{toMatrix}\,b = (\mathbf{M}(b))^\top$ where $\mathbf{M}(b)_{ij} = b(i)(j)$. Step 2: $b.\mathrm{toMatrix}\,e \cdot e.\mathrm{toMatrix}\,b = I_n$ (change-of-basis identity). Step 3: $\det(b.\mathrm{toMatrix}\,e) \cdot \det(\mathbf{M}(b)) = 1$ (product formula + transpose invariance of det). Conclude $\det(\mathbf{M}(b)) \neq 0$.

title: Converse Conversion: Module.Basis → Custom Lattice
content: Part 2 defines `latticeOfBasis`, the inverse map of the equivalence. Given `b : Module.Basis (Fin n) ℝ (Fin n → ℝ)`, it constructs a `Lattice n` by setting `basis := Matrix.of b` and using `basis_matrix_det_ne_zero n b` as the nonzero-determinant witness. The `noncomputable` keyword is required because `basis_matrix_det_ne_zero` uses classical reasoning (specifically the contradiction step) to produce the proof term. This definition shows the custom Lattice type is no more restrictive than Module.Basis: every abstract Mathlib basis gives a valid explicit-matrix lattice.
mathContext: $\mathrm{latticeOfBasis}(b) = \bigl(\mathbf{M}(b),\; \mathrm{basis\_matrix\_det\_ne\_zero}(b)\bigr) \in \text{Lattice}\,n$ where $\mathbf{M}(b)_{ij} = b(i)(j)$. This makes the diagram $\text{Module.Basis} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{latticeOfBasis}} \text{Lattice}\,n \xrightarrow{\mathrm{toModuleBasis}} \text{Module.Basis}$ well-defined.

title: Linear Equivalence Infrastructure: The Forward Map
content: Part 3 builds the forward map from custom Lattice to Module.Basis. First, `Lattice.toLinearEquiv` (lines 92–105) constructs a linear equivalence `(Fin n → ℝ) ≃ₗ[ℝ] (Fin n → ℝ)` by applying `LinearEquiv.ofBijective` to `L.basis.transpose.mulVecLin` (the linear map given by multiplication by `L.basisᵀ`). Injectivity follows from `Matrix.mulVec_injective_of_invertible` (since `L.basisᵀ` is invertible), and surjectivity from `Matrix.mulVec_surjective_of_invertible`. Second, `Lattice.toModuleBasis` (lines 106–108) pushes the standard basis along this equivalence: `(Pi.basisFun ℝ (Fin n)).map (L.toLinearEquiv n)`. Third, `Lattice.toModuleBasis_matrix_eq` (lines 110–119) proves the key structural identity: `Matrix.of (L.toModuleBasis n) = L.basis`, showing the matrix representation is preserved by the forward map.
mathContext: $L.\mathrm{toLinearEquiv}\,n : \mathbb{R}^n \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb{R}^n$ via $v \mapsto L.\mathrm{basis}^\top \cdot v$. Then $L.\mathrm{toModuleBasis}\,n = e.\mathrm{map}(L.\mathrm{toLinearEquiv}\,n)$ where $e = \mathrm{Pi.basisFun}$. Matrix preservation: $(L.\mathrm{toModuleBasis}\,n)(i)(j) = (L.\mathrm{toLinearEquiv}\,n(e_i))(j) = (L.\mathrm{basis}^\top \cdot e_i)(j) = L.\mathrm{basis}_{ij}$.

title: Round-Trip Identities: Proving the Bijection
content: Part 4 proves the two round-trip identities that establish `latticeOfBasis` and `toModuleBasis` are mutual inverses. `toModuleBasis_latticeOfBasis` (lines 126–135) proves `latticeOfBasis n (L.toModuleBasis n) = L`. It destructs `L` to access its fields and uses `Lattice.mk.injEq` to reduce the goal to matrix equality, which is supplied directly by `Lattice.toModuleBasis_matrix_eq`. `latticeOfBasis_toModuleBasis` (lines 137–149) proves `(latticeOfBasis n b).toModuleBasis n = b`. It first establishes matrix equality `Matrix.of ((latticeOfBasis n b).toModuleBasis n) = Matrix.of b` by chaining `toModuleBasis_matrix_eq` and the definition of `latticeOfBasis` (which sets `basis := Matrix.of b`). It then applies `DFunLike.ext` and `funext` to lift matrix equality to basis equality coordinate-wise.
mathContext: Round-trip 1 (Lattice side): $\mathrm{latticeOfBasis}(L.\mathrm{toModuleBasis}\,n) = L$. Proof: $\mathbf{M}(\mathrm{latticeOfBasis}(L.\mathrm{toModuleBasis}\,n)) = \mathbf{M}(L.\mathrm{toModuleBasis}\,n) = L.\mathrm{basis}$, so the structures agree. Round-trip 2 (Basis side): $(\mathrm{latticeOfBasis}(b)).\mathrm{toModuleBasis}\,n = b$. Proof: $\mathbf{M}(\text{LHS}) = \mathbf{M}(b)$ (by definition + toModuleBasis_matrix_eq), hence LHS and $b$ agree on all coordinates.

title: The Type Equivalence: Lattice n ≃ Module.Basis
content: Part 5 assembles everything into `latticeEquivBasis : Lattice n ≃ Module.Basis (Fin n) ℝ (Fin n → ℝ)`. This is a noncomputable equivalence of types whose `toFun` is `L.toModuleBasis n`, `invFun` is `latticeOfBasis n b`, `left_inv` is `toModuleBasis_latticeOfBasis`, and `right_inv` is `latticeOfBasis_toModuleBasis`. The docstring emphasizes the mathematical meaning: the custom API (explicit matrix with determinant condition, covolume = |det|) and the Mathlib API (abstract basis vectors, covolume via fundamental domain volume) are two descriptions of the same object. The `noncomputable` keyword reflects the use of classical choice in `toLinearEquiv` — the equivalence is canonical and constructive at the mathematical level, but not decidably computable in Lean's type theory.
mathContext: $\varphi : \text{Lattice}\,n \xrightarrow{\sim} \text{Basis}(\text{Fin}\,n, \mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R}^n)$, $\quad \varphi(L) = L.\mathrm{toModuleBasis}\,n$, $\quad \varphi^{-1}(b) = \mathrm{latticeOfBasis}\,n\,b$. This is an equivalence of types (not merely a bijection of sets), meaning it transports any type-theoretic structure on one side to the other. In particular, any theorem about `Lattice n` whose statement can be formulated using only the abstract type can be transferred to a statement about `Module.Basis` via `latticeEquivBasis`.
